items.prompt: With `int a = 10; int b = 3;`, what does `Console.WriteLine(a / b)` print, and what is the lesson's fix when you want the fractional result?
items.answer: 3, since int / int truncates; cast an operand first, `(double)a / b`, to get 3.333...
distractors: 3.3333333333333335, because the / operator always promotes its result to double in C#
3.33, because C# rounds division results to two decimal places unless told otherwise
4, because integer division rounds to the nearest whole number; use Math.Floor to get 3
items.explanation: Both operands are int, so the division is integer division (10 / 3 = 3). Casting one operand to double forces floating-point division.

items.prompt: The lesson stores `money` as `decimal 99.99m` but `precise` as `double`. Why is decimal the right type for prices?
items.answer: decimal stores base-10 fractions like 0.01 exactly, while double's binary rounding loses pennies
distractors: double cannot store numbers with more than two digits after the decimal point without truncating
decimal arithmetic is faster than double arithmetic, which matters on busy checkout pages
the m suffix makes every decimal result round automatically to two places, like a price
items.explanation: The lesson labels double 'not for money' and decimal 'exact money (never lose pennies!)'; the m suffix only makes the literal a decimal.

items.prompt: A user types "abc". Compare `int.Parse` with line 52's `int.TryParse("abc", out int parsed) ? parsed : 0`.
items.answer: int.Parse throws a FormatException; TryParse returns false and the ternary falls back to 0
distractors: Both return 0 for non-numeric input; TryParse only differs by also reporting whether it succeeded
int.Parse returns null and TryParse throws, which is why line 52 needs the ternary
Both throw FormatException; TryParse just puts the message into its out variable
items.explanation: 11-exception-handling catches exactly this FormatException from int.Parse("abc"); TryParse reports failure through its bool return instead.

items.prompt: `Snack a = new() { Name = "old" }; Snack b = a; b.Name = "new"; Console.WriteLine(a.Name);` What is printed, and why does `int b = a; b = 99;` behave differently?
items.answer: new: class assignment copies a reference to one object, but an int copy is independent
distractors: old: assigning a class instance copies the whole object, just like assigning an int does
old: b = a copies the object, and Name is a field, so it is never shared between copies
It does not compile: a class instance cannot be assigned to a second variable without new
items.explanation: The bug-hunt files contrast value copies (int a stays 10) with reference sharing (a.Name changes to "new").

items.prompt: `string s = "test"; s.ToUpper(); Console.WriteLine(s);` What is printed, and what is the one-line fix?
items.answer: test: strings are immutable and the new string was discarded; fix with s = s.ToUpper()
distractors: TEST, because ToUpper rewrites the characters of s in place, so no assignment is needed
Nothing compiles: ignoring the return value of a string method is a compile error in C#
An empty line, because ToUpper moves the text into a new string and clears the original
items.explanation: String methods never modify the original; the bug-hunt marks the ignored result, and the think-predict prints s unchanged after Trim().ToLower().

items.prompt: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.Speak();` prints Woof. If Dog had declared `public new void Speak()` instead of `override`, what would the same call print?
items.answer: "...": new only hides Animal.Speak, so an Animal-typed call still runs Animal's version
distractors: Woof, because the runtime always calls the method of the object's actual type, new or not
Woof twice, because a new method runs the derived version after the base version
Nothing compiles: a virtual method can only be redeclared in a subclass with override
items.explanation: The bug-hunt warns that forgetting override leads to hiding instead of polymorphism; only override replaces the virtual slot.

items.prompt: Predict the output of the think-predict block that calls `int.Parse("abc")` inside try, with `catch (FormatException)` and a finally.
items.answer: "bad format" then "always": catch handles the FormatException, then finally runs
distractors: Only "always": when a finally block is present, it replaces the catch block entirely
"always" then "bad format": finally runs as soon as the exception is thrown, before catch
"always" and then an unhandled FormatException crash, because finally rethrows
items.explanation: The matching catch runs first; finally runs after the try/catch regardless of whether an exception happened.

items.prompt: In STEP 3, `var task1 = GetDataAsync(); var task2 = GetDataAsync(); await Task.WhenAll(task1, task2);` Each call delays 1000 ms. When does the work start, and roughly how long does the block take?
items.answer: Each starts when GetDataAsync() is called, so the delays overlap; WhenAll only awaits, ~1s
distractors: Nothing starts until Task.WhenAll, which then launches both tasks in parallel, about 1 second
task2 cannot start until task1 has been awaited, so the whole block takes about 2 seconds
Neither task runs at all, because tasks returned by async methods must be started with Start()
items.explanation: Calling an async method runs it until its first await and returns a hot task; WhenAll just waits for both.

items.prompt: Why do the lesson and its bug hunt warn against calling `.Result` or `.Wait()` on a task?
items.answer: They block the thread, and if the continuation needs that thread, both wait forever
distractors: They return the task's value before it finishes, so you may read a default value
They turn the caller into async void, so any exception thrown by the task is lost
They cancel the task after a default 30-second timeout, returning partial results
items.explanation: Sync-over-async blocks a thread the awaited continuation may need; awaiting all the way up avoids the deadlock.

items.prompt: In the think-predict, suppose `nums[1] = 6;` were inserted between the line that builds `evens` and the `string.Join` line. What would be printed?
items.answer: 60,40: the query is deferred and runs only when string.Join enumerates the updated array
distractors: 20,40, because the Where/Select query captured its results at the moment evens was assigned
20,60,40, because the query keeps its earlier results and appends any new matches
An InvalidOperationException, because the array was modified after the query was built
items.explanation: Deferred execution: the query does not run until it is materialized or enumerated (ToList, foreach, string.Join...).

items.prompt: An `IEnumerable<Order>` built from a database query is passed to `.Count()` and then to a `foreach`. What does the bug hunt say goes wrong, and what is the fix?
items.answer: The query runs twice, hitting the database twice; call ToList() once and reuse the list
distractors: The foreach throws, because an IEnumerable can only be enumerated once after Count() reads it
Nothing goes wrong: Count() caches the results, so the foreach reads them from memory
The foreach skips the items that Count() already read, so the loop sees an empty sequence
items.explanation: Each enumeration of a deferred query re-runs it; ToList() makes one materialized copy.

items.prompt: After `var p2 = p1 with { Age = 29 };`, a third record is made with `var p3 = p2 with { Age = 28 };` (p1's original age). What does `p1 == p3` print?
items.answer: True: records get compiler-generated value equality, so equal properties compare equal
distractors: False, because == compares references and p3 is a different object from p1 in memory
False, because a with-expression copy remembers that it was derived from p2, not p1
Nothing compiles: the == operator is not defined for record types, so you must call Equals
items.explanation: The compiler generates Equals/GetHashCode/== for records; p1 == p2 is False only because the ages differ.

items.prompt: `string? name = null; ... string definitelyNotNull = name!;` What does the `!` actually do, and what happens if code later reads `definitelyNotNull.Length`?
items.answer: It only silences the nullable warning; the value is still null, so .Length throws
distractors: It throws immediately on that line, because name is null when the ! is applied
It converts null into an empty string, so .Length returns 0 instead of throwing
It makes the compiler add a runtime null check that substitutes a default value
items.explanation: The null-forgiving operator is a compile-time promise with no runtime effect; overusing it defeats nullable reference types.

items.prompt: Outside the Button class, code tries `button.Clicked(button, EventArgs.Empty);` to fake a click. What happens, and what may outside code do with Clicked?
items.answer: It does not compile: only the declaring class can raise an event; outsiders use += and -=
distractors: It compiles and raises the event, since Clicked is declared public on the Button class
It compiles but throws a NullReferenceException at runtime, because nothing has subscribed yet
It compiles only if written Clicked?.Invoke, which makes it safe to call from anywhere
items.explanation: The lesson: an event is a delegate that can only be invoked from inside the class, so only the owner can raise it.

items.front: `string maybe = null; Console.WriteLine(maybe.Length);` What happens, and what are two safe alternatives?
items.back: NullReferenceException at runtime. Guard it: maybe?.Length ?? 0, or string.IsNullOrEmpty(maybe) before reading Length.

items.front: Three exception-handling bugs from the bug hunt: an empty catch (Exception), missing using on disposables, and throwing inside finally. Why is the last one so nasty?
items.back: An exception thrown in finally replaces the one already propagating, so the real root cause is lost from logs and callers.

items.front: Why is `async void` on a normal method a bug (outside event handlers)?
items.back: The caller gets no Task, so it cannot await it or observe failures; an exception escapes onto the synchronization context and can crash the process. Return Task instead.

items.front: LINQ bug hunt: First() vs FirstOrDefault() when nothing matches?
items.back: First() throws InvalidOperationException; FirstOrDefault() returns default (null for reference types), which the caller must then handle.

items.front: Two event mistakes from the delegates lesson, and the pattern that avoids the second?
items.back: Not unsubscribing (the publisher keeps the subscriber alive: a memory leak) and raising without a null check; raise with Clicked?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty).
